scope_note: Routing follows the pr-loop scope boundary: HIGH/MEDIUM findings block only when they violate the task's acceptance criteria, turn the gate red, or make a published number or claim dishonest. R7 is LOW but routed `repair` because fixing R3 without it would leave README and analysis.md citing different 'current' reports — a new inconsistency created by the repair itself.

findings.route_reason: ADR-010 Decision 2 publishes the claim 'The ceiling is enforced, not asserted'. The reviewer demonstrated a 77.23s suite reporting PASS and 1.000 in a fresh clone, which is how CI runs. The published claim is materially dishonest as written.
findings.claim: `fast-wall-clock-budget` cannot go red in CI — the gate CLAUDE.md and .github/workflows/eval.yml treat as authoritative — because it grades a committed report file instead of the run it is part of, so a tree whose `fast` suite is 28% over the ceiling still reports PASS and 1.000.
findings.evidence: src/browser/eval_adapter.py:1039-1052 (`_run_wall_clock_case`) reads `sorted(evals/report/*-fast.json)[-1]` and nothing else. `.github/workflows/eval.yml` runs `actions/checkout` then `python -m evals.run --suite fast`, so the newest file in a fresh clone is always the committed `evals/report/20260821-114704-fast.json` (wall 54.35). The current run's own timing is never consulted, and the report it writes lands after the run and is discarded with the workspace. The case's `not_covered` discloses only the `--no-report` hole, not the fresh-clone/CI one.
findings.repro: Fresh clone of b8215fd, wrap `evals.run.run_case` to add 0.25s per case (no repo file edited), then `python -m evals.run --suite fast --no-report`. Observed: `[PASS] fast-wall-clock-budget (adversarial, 0.26s)` / `suite 'fast': 89/89 = 1.000` / `wall 77.23s` — 17.2s over the 60s ceiling, gate green.
findings.acceptance: Either the case reads the run it belongs to (e.g. the runner exposes elapsed-so-far, or the ceiling is checked in `evals/run.py` against `totals.wall_seconds` before it writes the report), or ADR-010 Decision 2 and the case's `not_covered` state plainly that the check is inert in CI and on any fresh checkout, and name what does enforce the ceiling there.

findings.route_reason: The PR introduces a new failure mode in which one case's crash makes every subsequent case fail under its own name — the suite would count and attribute wrong. Routed repair rather than declared-not-fixed because the repo's own history (support-matrix D3) is that 'no fixture shows this shape' gets falsified within days, and the guard is one line.
findings.claim: `_browser()` only checks `is None`, so once the shared Chromium dies every remaining case in the process is handed the dead object and fails with `TargetClosedError` attributed to itself — a single-case fault now cascades across the suite, which per-case launches previously contained.
findings.evidence: src/browser/eval_adapter.py:100-112 — `if _BROWSER is None:` is the only liveness test; a closed/crashed browser is not None and is returned forever. ADR-010 Decision 1 and the `run_task` docstring (src/browser/agent.py:263-271) assert "Isolation is unchanged", which is true only for cookies/storage, not for process-level fault isolation. `agent-launches-its-own-browser`'s own `triage.not_covered` concedes "nothing pins isolation itself".
findings.repro: Driver against the worktree adapter: run `tc1-hello-heading` (PASS), then `_await(_BROWSER.close())` to simulate the Chromium dying, then run `tc5-forms-submit` and `tc1-shop-price`. Both fail: `TargetClosedError: Browser.new_context: Target page, context or browser has been closed`, and `_BROWSER is None` is still False.
findings.acceptance: `_browser()` re-launches when `_BROWSER.is_connected()` is false (one line), or an adversarial case pins the intended behavior after a shared-browser death and the ADR's "isolation is unchanged" is narrowed to cookies/storage in writing.

findings.route_reason: Directly dishonest published numbers, in a document whose own preamble promises every number is read out of a committed report — and the stale figures sit immediately under a note this PR adds claiming only two figures moved.
findings.claim: docs/analysis.md still publishes two figures this PR moved — "168 browser actions in a `fast` run" and "53 of the 86 cases" — immediately under a note the PR adds asserting that exactly two figures moved, so the documents of record contradict the PR's own published numbers (170 actions, 89 cases).
findings.evidence: docs/analysis.md:33-39: the added note says "Two of them have since moved and are not restated across this document: M12 put `fast` at 89/89 in 54.7s ... and `invariant` at 23/23", and lines 38-39 then read "96 distinct cases (20 golden + 76 adversarial). / 168 browser actions in a `fast` run; **53 of the 86** cases". ADR-010, README.md:56 and the case provenance all publish 170 actions / 89 cases; `ls evals/{golden,adversarial}/*.json` is 20 + 79 = 99 distinct cases. analysis.md's own preamble says "Every number below is read out of a committed report ... Where a number does not exist, this document says so".
findings.repro: `python -m evals.run --suite fast --no-report` in the worktree → `89/89 ... 170 actions`; compare with docs/analysis.md:38-39. `ls evals/golden/*.json evals/adversarial/*.json | wc -l` → 99.
findings.acceptance: Either the 168/86/96 figures are restated from `evals/report/20260821-114704-fast.json`, or the added note enumerates every figure it knows to be stale rather than claiming only two moved.

findings.route_reason: LOW and no figure is wrong, so it does not block on its own. Folded into R3 because repairing R3 against the newest committed report while README cites an older one would create a fresh contradiction between the two documents of record.
findings.claim: README's "Latest offline baseline" cites an older run than the newest report the branch commits, which is also the report the new gate actually reads.
findings.evidence: README.md:52 cites `evals/report/20260821-024150-fast.json` (54.74s); the commit also adds `evals/report/20260821-114704-fast.json` (54.35s, 89/89, same metrics), and `fast-wall-clock-budget` grades that newer one. No published figure is wrong — both runs are 1.000 with identical derived numbers — but the document of record and the enforcement point disagree on which run is current.
findings.acceptance: README cites the newest committed fast/invariant/live triple, or says why an earlier one is the cited baseline.

findings.route_reason: LOW; the wording half is naturally corrected by R1's repair, the zero-case-refusal half is a separate hardening with no demonstrated trigger.
findings.claim: `_run_wall_clock_case`'s docstring and both case notes say "newest **committed**" report, but the glob reads the working tree, so any untracked file — a scratch run, an experiment from another branch, a hand-written file — silently decides the verdict, and no sanity check rejects a report that graded zero cases.
findings.evidence: src/browser/eval_adapter.py:1045 globs the filesystem with no git awareness; the returned `got` includes `"cases": 0` for an empty report without complaint. Filenames are stamped from the local clock (evals/run.py:135), so a skewed clock writes a file that permanently wins `sorted(...)[-1]`.
findings.repro: In a clone of b8215fd, write `evals/report/29991231-235959-fast.json` containing `{"totals":{"wall_seconds":999.0},"results":[]}` (untracked, `git status` shows `??`), then run the case: `{'passed': False, 'got': {'report': '29991231-235959-fast.json', 'wall_seconds': 999.0, 'budget': 60, 'cases': 0}}`.
findings.acceptance: Wording says "newest report in evals/report/" rather than "committed", or the case reads git-tracked files only; and it refuses a report with `len(results) == 0` as unmeasured rather than grading it.

findings.route_reason: LOW and unreachable from any committed case; a full run in reversed order leaks zero contexts.
findings.claim: On the borrowed-browser path a `BrowserContext` is created outside the `try`, so a failure in `ctx.new_page()` leaks that context for the life of the eval process; the own-browser path is covered only incidentally by the exit stack.
findings.evidence: src/browser/agent.py:311-312 — `ctx = await browser.new_context()` and `page = await ctx.new_page()` precede the `try:` whose `finally: await ctx.close()` (line 567-568) is the only close. When `browser` was borrowed there is no `stack.push_async_callback(browser.close)` to sweep it up.
findings.repro: Not reachable from a committed case (a full `fast` run in reverse case order leaves `len(_BROWSER.contexts) == 0`); reachable by making `ctx.new_page()` raise on the shared path.
findings.acceptance: `ctx` is created inside the exit stack (`stack.push_async_callback(ctx.close)`) or inside the `try`, so both paths close it on any failure.

findings.route_reason: LOW and a workflow-ergonomics question rather than a correctness one, but a real one: it decides what a contributor on slower hardware is supposed to do, which is a policy call for the repo owner rather than something to improvise inside this PR.
findings.claim: ADR-010 justifies keeping the wall-clock case out of `invariant` because a wall clock is machine-dependent, but places it in `fast`, which is hard-gated at baseline 1.000 — so a contributor whose machine measures >60s is blocked from committing with no sanctioned escape.
findings.evidence: evals/adversarial/fast-wall-clock-budget.json `suites: ["fast"]`; `.eval-baseline.json` is `{"fast": 1.0}` and `.githooks/pre-commit` exits 1 on `score < baseline`. ADR-009 Decision 6 (quoted in the case's own triage note) records the same suite at 68.6s on a reviewer's machine. CLAUDE.md hard rule 1 forbids `--update-baseline` to clear a gate, and rule 5 makes `--no-verify` an emergency.
findings.repro: The 0.25s-per-case slowdown run above writes a 77.23s report; the next `fast` run on that machine reads it and returns `88/89 = 0.989 < baseline 1.000`, blocking every commit until the report is deleted.
findings.acceptance: ADR-010 names the escape hatch for a slow machine (delete the report / an env-var override / a per-machine calibration factor), or the ceiling is expressed as something machine-independent (e.g. summed deliberate-wait budget, or per-case counts).

not_falsified: ADR-010's 11.3s / 42.2s / 13.5s split is internally consistent and sums to 67.0
every derived figure reproduces: 89/89 = 1.000, 170 actions, wall 54.37s, recovery 7/7, mutation 9/11 (6 recovered / 5 relocating), diagnosis 14/14, 4 replans; invariant 23/23
agent-launches-its-own-browser genuinely takes the production launch path (passes when _browser() is patched to raise, while tc1-hello-heading fails under the same patch)
fast-wall-clock-budget's watched-red evidence is committed and reproducible (20260821-022406-fast.json and -022629-fast.json record it false with the pre-fix wall_seconds)
no ordering dependence or storage crossover: all 89 cases in reversed order still 89/89 with zero leaked BrowserContexts
no orphan Chromium or Playwright driver process survives the run despite _LOOP/_BROWSER never being closed
headless is only passed by src/browser/cli.py:26, which always leaves browser=None, so no caller is affected by it being ignored on the borrowed path
no production constant bent, no case deleted, no suite-tag move present in the diff
